structure: Left: an independent clause ending on 'orchard'. Right: an independent clause whose subject 'a sheltered block of trees planted by the previous owner' reads as an appositive of 'orchard' until its verb 'flowered' (10th word after the blank).

distractor_pulls.orchard, a: For nine words the noun phrase is a perfect appositive: an orchard IS a block of trees planted by a previous owner, so a comma looks exactly right.
distractor_pulls.orchard a: A reader who takes 'a sheltered block of trees' as a restrictive identifier of the orchard, or who loses track of the long sentence, leaves the words unpunctuated.
distractor_pulls.orchard: a: A colon often introduces a description of the noun just before it; a reader who reads the noun phrase as a definition of the orchard and accepts what follows as elaboration of the move picks the colon.

distractor_kills.orchard, a: Comma splice: 'a sheltered block of trees planted by the previous owner flowered eleven days later' is an independent clause. The comma would be correct only if 'flowered' were removed (a true appositive).
distractor_kills.orchard a: Fused sentence: two independent clauses with no punctuation or conjunction.
distractor_kills.orchard: a: A colon joining two clauses requires the second to explain, list, or restate the first; the flowering eleven days later is a later, separate event, not an explanation of the move. A colon would be right before a clause such as 'the trees there flowered first', which explains the choice.

frame: Opening 'In herds enrolled in the trial,' (plural); subject 'the treated cows' milk from any quarter that the veterinarian injected with the new antibiotic' (plural possessive 'cows'' in front of the singular mass head 'milk'; a past object relative 'injected' inside the subject); 'is kept' vs 'was kept' settled by a present unless-clause 6 words after the blank
decider_quote: unless a laboratory test of that quarter comes back free of the drug
deletion_test: Delete the unless-clause and 'the treated cows' milk ... was kept out of the bulk tank' (a past report, matching 'injected') is as correct as 'is kept'; tense becomes undecidable.

distractor_pulls.was kept: Everything around the blank is past: the trial is narrated in the past, and the verb right inside the subject is the past 'injected'; the singular past continues that report.
distractor_pulls.were kept: The subject opens on the plural possessive 'the treated cows'', and the sentence opens on 'herds'; a student who reads the cows as what is withheld, in a past report, picks the plural past.
distractor_pulls.are kept: A student who hears the present 'comes back' but takes 'the treated cows'' as the head (it is the first noun of the subject) picks the plural present.

distractor_kills.was kept: Sequence of tenses: a past main verb with 'unless ... comes back' (present) is inconsistent; 'was kept' would be correct only with 'unless a laboratory test ... came back'. The past 'injected' is inside a relative clause and does not set the main verb's tense.
distractor_kills.were kept: Subject-verb agreement (the head 'milk' is singular; 'cows'' is a possessive determiner) and tense (present 'comes back').
distractor_kills.are kept: Subject-verb agreement: 'cows'' only modifies 'milk'; 'are kept' would be correct only with 'the treated cows ... are kept'.

heuristics_that_give_key: the key is the uniquely shortest option (counted against the 3-per-author cap)

frame: Opening 'Though a bank's barley samples rarely ___,' (first noun 'bank's' singular possessive; head 'samples' plural); the elided verb is the main clause's LEXICAL 'has trouble sprouting' (10 words after the blank), which takes do in ellipsis, so the printed 'has' lures 'have'; main subject 'a typical sample of onion seed' singular
deletion_test: Replace 'has trouble sprouting' with a perfect ('has lost its ability to sprout') and 'have' becomes correct; with no main verb to copy, do vs have is undecidable.

distractor_pulls.rarely does: The first noun after the blank, 'a typical sample', is singular, and so is the sentence's first noun 'bank's'; a student matching the auxiliary to the subject of the clause that completes the thought picks 'does'.
distractor_pulls.rarely have: The main clause prints 'has', and the ellipsis rule students learn is 'copy the other clause's verb'; 'rarely have' copies it exactly and agrees with 'samples'.
distractor_pulls.rarely has: A student who copies the printed 'has' and matches it to the singular 'sample' or 'bank's' picks 'rarely has'.

distractor_kills.rarely does: Subject-verb agreement: the opening clause's subject is 'samples' (plural); 'does' would be correct only with 'a bank's barley sample'.
distractor_kills.rarely have: Ellipsis: 'has' in 'has trouble sprouting' is a main verb (experience), and a main-verb 'have' takes do-support when its predicate is omitted; an auxiliary 'have' can stand only for a perfect. 'have' would be correct only if the main clause read 'has lost much of its ability to sprout'.

frame: Sentence 1 (of the blank pair) ends 'families skipping the last dose'; sentence 2 opens 'A booster given months after the others, when children are toddlers and harder to find,' which is a TRUE appositive of 'the last dose' until 'turned out' arrives (15th word after the blank); sentence 2 is a finding that runs against the worry, not an explanation. New setting (malaria vaccine field trial) and skeleton per the template-partner rule
structure: Left: a complete compound sentence ending on 'dose'. Right: an independent clause whose long subject (noun + participial phrase + when-clause) renames the last dose until its verb 'turned out'.
decider_quote: turned out to raise antibody levels

distractor_pulls.dose, a: The last dose IS the booster given months after the others, so a comma appositive reads as accurate information for fourteen words, through an internal clause, until 'turned out'.
distractor_pulls.dose: a: 'worried most about ... the last dose' sets up a specification, and a colon commonly introduces the thing named; a reader who takes 'a booster given months after the others' as that specification picks the colon.
distractor_pulls.dose a: A reader who loses the structure in the long sentence, or reads the booster phrase as tightly bound to 'dose', leaves it unpunctuated.

distractor_kills.dose, a: Comma splice: 'A booster ... turned out to raise antibody levels far more than any earlier injection' is an independent clause; the comma would be right only without 'turned out to raise ...'.
distractor_kills.dose: a: A colon joining two clauses requires the second to explain, list, or restate the first; this clause reports a separate result (the booster raised antibodies most) that runs against the worry, not an explanation of why the organizers worried. A colon would be right before the phrase alone, with no verb.
distractor_kills.dose a: Fused sentence: two independent clauses with no punctuation.

frame: Fronted 'Wired to a logger at the edge of a hillside estate,' (singular nouns); head 'probes' (not the first noun of the sentence); object is an embedded clause 'how many liters of water the clay loses each day', after which 'for nine growing seasons' (11 words after the blank) must be attached to the main verb, settling 'have been measuring' over 'are measuring'
deletion_test: Delete 'for nine growing seasons' and 'the moisture probes ... are measuring how many liters of water the clay loses each day' is as correct as 'have been measuring'; aspect becomes undecidable.

distractor_pulls.has been measuring: The sentence opens on singular nouns ('a logger', 'a hillside estate'), and a logger is what records; a student who takes the wired logger as the actor and hears the duration picks the singular perfect.
distractor_pulls.are measuring: The probes measure right now and 'their readings show' in the present; and the duration seems to belong to the embedded clause ('the clay loses each day for nine growing seasons'), so the plain present progressive looks untouched by it.
distractor_pulls.is measuring: A student who attaches the duration to the embedded clause and takes the logger as the subject picks the singular present progressive.

distractor_kills.has been measuring: Subject-verb agreement: the head is 'probes' (plural); the fronted phrase's nouns cannot be the subject. It would be right only with 'the moisture probe beside its oldest vine'.
distractor_kills.are measuring: Aspect: 'for nine growing seasons' can modify only the main verb (a simple present 'loses each day' does not take a span of seasons), and an activity over a stated span up to the present requires the present perfect progressive; 'are measuring' would be right only without the duration phrase.

heuristics_that_give_key: duration phrase -> perfect (the row's one duration cue, by design; it now has to be attached past an embedded clause)

frame: Previous sentence names the plural owner 'broiler chicks'; blank sentence 'At the region's largest grower, the flock veterinarian and the vaccine maker's field technicians ___ antibody levels'; the verb takes the compound (plural; first member singular), the pronoun takes 'chicks'; singular 'flock' and 'vaccine' sit inside modifiers and cannot own the levels
deletion_test: Replace 'broiler chicks' with 'a broiler chick' (and 'the birds inhale' with 'the bird inhales') and 'its' becomes correct; without the previous sentence the levels have no owner and its/their is undecidable.

distractor_pulls.has measured their: The subject opens on the singular 'the flock veterinarian', the one professional responsible for a flock; a student who stops at that noun gives the verb the singular and the pronoun the chicks.
distractor_pulls.have measured its: Antibody levels are reported per flock ('the flock's antibody level') or per vaccine ('the vaccine's antibody response'), and both words sit in the subject; a student who copies the plural to the verb and takes the flock or the vaccine as owner picks 'its'.
distractor_pulls.has measured its: A student who reads 'the flock veterinarian' as the subject and the flock as the owner makes both singular.

distractor_kills.has measured their: Subject-verb agreement: two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb; 'has' would be right only with 'the flock veterinarian' alone.
distractor_kills.have measured its: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: the owner of the antibody levels is 'broiler chicks' (plural, previous sentence); 'flock' and 'vaccine' are noun modifiers ('flock veterinarian', 'vaccine maker's') and cannot be antecedents. 'its' would be right only if the previous sentence named 'a broiler chick'.
distractor_kills.has measured its: Both agreements fail: compound plural subject and plural antecedent.

frame: Subject 'Certain species of French marigold that the agronomists sowed along each row': head 'species' has identical singular and plural forms and is made plural only by 'Certain' (H3: skipping to the head does not give the number); past relative 'sowed' and singular 'marigold', 'row' before the blank; 'are holding' vs 'were holding' settled by the present conditional 6 words after the blank

distractor_pulls.is holding: 'species' looks like any singular -s word ('a species'), and the nouns right before the blank are the singular 'marigold' and 'row'; a student who reads one kind of marigold as the subject picks the singular present.
distractor_pulls.were holding: The fieldwork is reported in the past and the verb inside the subject is the past 'sowed'; the plural past continues that report.
distractor_pulls.was holding: A student who follows the past narration and reads 'species' as singular picks the singular past.

distractor_kills.is holding: Subject-verb agreement: 'Certain' requires a plural noun, so 'species' is plural here; 'is holding' would be right only with 'A certain species'.
distractor_kills.were holding: Sequence of tenses: a past main verb with 'as long as a bed is not planted' (present) is inconsistent; 'were holding' would be right only with 'as long as a bed was not planted'. 'sowed' is inside a relative clause and does not set the main verb's tense.

frame: 'the auditors found' + content clause with 'that' omitted; its subject 'the hand-rub bottles that nurses carry clipped to their uniforms' contains its own finite verb 'carry' and a small-clause participle 'clipped', so the words read as a finished object until 'were used' (10th word after the blank)
structure: Left: 'the auditors found', a verb needing an object. Right: a content clause (that omitted) whose subject contains a relative clause with its own verb ('carry'); the clause's verb 'were used' is delayed.
decider_quote: were used far less often than the sinks

distractor_pulls.found—the: A dash often introduces a revealed finding, and the sentence builds to a surprise; a reader who hears 'the hand-rub bottles that nurses carry ... were used far less often' as a dramatic reveal picks the dash.
distractor_pulls.found, the: A reader pauses after a reporting verb, and the first verb reached after it, 'carry', makes the words look like the start of a separate clause set off from the sentence frame.
distractor_pulls.found; the: A reader who takes 'the hand-rub bottles ... were used far less often' as an independent clause and treats 'the auditors found' as a report verb that needs nothing more joins two clauses.

distractor_kills.found—the: No punctuation between a verb and its object: the clause beginning 'the hand-rub bottles' is the object of 'found'. A dash would be right only after a complete clause, such as 'the auditors found something unexpected—the bottles ...'.
distractor_kills.found, the: A comma may not separate a verb from its object clause; it would be right only before a nonessential element.
distractor_kills.found; the: A semicolon must follow an independent clause; 'When ..., the auditors found' is incomplete because 'found' needs an object here.

frame: Opening 'Although in most growing regions the standard fungicide program usually ___,' (first noun 'regions' plural, head 'program' singular); the elided predicate is the main clause's 'hardly dependable', whose 'are' is split from it by 'against the newest strains of the fungus' (adjective 18 words after the blank); the next sentence's lexical 'evolve' pulls 'does'; main subject 'the genes' plural. distractor_pulls.usually does: A student who finds the singular 'program' but reads it as habitually doing something (working, holding) supplies the do-auxiliary.

distractor_kills.usually do: Ellipsis (the omitted predicate is the adjective 'dependable', which needs 'be') and agreement (singular 'program').
distractor_kills.usually does: Ellipsis: 'does' can stand only for a lexical verb; the omitted predicate is 'hardly dependable', so the elided form is 'is dependable'. 'does' would be right only if the main clause read 'rarely hold up against the newest strains'.

frame: 'the ___ graft of a rare papershell cultivar onto a seedling rootstock, the final join of a long career at the nursery, was the first to break bud'; one owner is inferred from 'a long career' (one career, one person) 13+ words after the blank, never from a word next to it; the previous sentence names 'propagators' (plural) to pull the plural possessive; 'graft' reads as a verb after a plain plural until 'was'

distractor_pulls.propagators': The previous sentence names 'propagators' in the plural as the staff who do this job, so 'the propagators' graft' reads as a reference back to them.

distractor_kills.propagator: A noun that owns the following noun must be possessive; 'the propagator graft' has no possessive marker and 'propagator graft' is not a compound.
